docs.title: detection rule gate
docs.text:
Fails a detection-as-code pull request when a Sigma rule is unmapped, unbounded or missing the context an analyst needs at 03:00.

Detection content gets reviewed by people reading YAML in a diff. Application code gets a linter. This is the linter.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Checks is every check, its default severity and how often it fires on a pinned corpus of 3,799 real Sigma rules. Generated from the registry, so it cannot drift from the code.
  • False positives is the part no benchmark can do. Three of the original check designs flagged correct Sigma, and the only way to find out was to read every finding one rule at a time. All three are written up with the per rule reasoning.
  • Limitations is what this deliberately does not do, each with the condition that would trigger building it.
  • Sources is where every allowed value comes from, pinned to a commit. The modifier allowlist was wrong the first time because it was written from memory.

docs.title: The design position in one paragraph
docs.text: A gate is only useful if it stays turned on. Every default severity here was set from how often the check fires on a real corpus rather than from how serious the finding sounds, because a check that fails the build on a quarter of a team's existing rules gets removed in its first week. A suppression requires a written reason, so the gate cannot be silenced quietly one rule at a time. And when a check turns out to flag correct content, that is published rather than patched out, because the failure rate of a check is the number that decides whether anyone trusts it.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install detection-rule-gate
drg check rules

Or as a GitHub Action, or a pre-commit hook. The readme has all three.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Generated by tools/generate_checks_doc.py from the check registry. Edit the rationale on the check, not this file.

Every default severity below was set from how often the check fires on the pinned public corpus of 3,799 Sigma rules, not from how serious the finding sounds. A check that fails the build on a quarter of a team's existing rules is a check that gets switched off in its first week, so a high firing rate argues for a warning default even where the finding is worth making. The rates are measured, and benchmark/run_benchmark.py reproduces them.

Two findings cannot be configured: a file that does not parse, and a file that parses and is not a Sigma rule. Neither can be assessed, and neither will load in a backend.

check default scope fires on corpus attack-technique-missing warning rule 470 (12.37%) broad-logsource warning rule 19 (0.5%) condition-undefined-selection error rule 0 (0.0%) condition-unparseable error rule 0 (0.0%) duplicate-rule-id error corpus 0 (0.0%) duplicate-yaml-key error rule 0 (0.0%) missing-falsepositives warning rule 949 (24.98%) missing-rule-id error rule 0 (0.0%) rule-invalid error file 0 (0.0%) rule-unparseable error file 0 (0.0%) suppression-unknown-check error file 0 (0.0%) suppression-without-reason error file 0 (0.0%) unbounded-selection warning rule 1 (0.03%) unknown-field-modifier error rule 0 (0.0%)

docs.title: attack-technique-missing
docs.text:
rule has no ATT&CK technique tag

A coverage review counts techniques. A rule tagged only with a tactic cannot be placed on a coverage matrix, cannot be compared against a threat profile, and cannot be found by anyone asking what detects a specific technique. Groups and software tags describe who, not what.

  • Default severity: warning
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 470 of the corpus (12.37%)

docs.title: broad-logsource
docs.text:
log source names a product with no category or service

The backend evaluates the rule against every event the product emits rather than one event channel, which multiplies the cost of the rule by the size of the estate. Add the category or the service the detection was written against.

  • Default severity: warning
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 19 of the corpus (0.5%)

docs.title: condition-undefined-selection
docs.text:
condition names a selection the rule does not define

A backend resolves the missing name to nothing, so the rule either matches everything or matches nothing depending on where the name sits in the condition. Neither failure announces itself: the rule deploys, runs, and is silently not the detection anyone reviewed.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)

docs.title: condition-unparseable
docs.text:
condition cannot be read

Either the condition is malformed, or it uses a form this tool does not implement. Both are worth stopping for: the first will not load in a backend, and the second means the checks that read the condition did not run on this rule, so the rule was not fully gated.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)

docs.title: duplicate-rule-id
docs.text:
two rules share an id

The id is what every downstream system uses to tell one rule from another, so a duplicate means one of the two is invisible to deduplication, to tracking, and to whichever system loads them in an order nobody controls.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: corpus
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)

docs.title: duplicate-yaml-key
docs.text:
the same key appears twice in one mapping

The YAML parser keeps the last value and discards the earlier one in silence. If the repeated key is a selection, half the detection was lost before any check could see it, and the rule will behave as though the first block was never written.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)

docs.title: missing-falsepositives
docs.text:
rule has no usable false positive note

The note is the handover to whoever triages the alert. An empty field, or the word Unknown, tells them the author did not know either, which is the moment a real detection starts being closed as noise. Name one thing that legitimately fires this rule, or say explicitly that nothing is expected to.

  • Default severity: warning
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 949 of the corpus (24.98%)
  • Options: levels (default ['high', 'critical'])

docs.title: missing-rule-id
docs.text:
rule has no id

Without a UUID the rule cannot be tracked across a rename, cited in a ticket, or matched against the upstream rule it came from. Generate one once and it never changes again.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)

docs.title: rule-invalid
docs.text:
file is valid YAML but not a Sigma rule

A required field is absent or has a value the specification does not allow. The rule will not load, so the remaining checks were not run against it.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: file
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)
  • Not configurable

docs.title: rule-unparseable
docs.text:
file is not loadable YAML

The file could not be parsed, so no other check ran against it. A backend will reject it for the same reason.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: file
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)
  • Not configurable

docs.title: suppression-unknown-check
docs.text:
suppression names a check that does not exist

The suppression applies to nothing, so the rule looks silenced and the gate still fires. A misspelled check id here is the quietest way to believe a finding was handled.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: file
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)
  • Not configurable

docs.title: suppression-without-reason
docs.text:
suppression comment gives no reason

Silencing a finding is a decision, and the person who benefits from it being written down is whoever reads the rule next year. Add 'reason: ' and a sentence after the check name.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: file
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)
  • Not configurable

docs.title: unbounded-selection
docs.text:
selection matches every event in the log source

Every constraint in this selection matches any value, and the condition makes the selection sufficient on its own, so the rule fires on everything the log source emits minus its filters. That may be deliberate for an allowlist style detection, in which case suppress it with the reason, so the next reviewer knows it was a decision.

  • Default severity: warning
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 1 of the corpus (0.03%)

docs.title: unknown-field-modifier
docs.text:
field uses a modifier the specification does not define

A misspelled modifier does not fail. It converts, deploys, runs and matches nothing, while the rule still appears in the coverage report. Check the spelling against the Sigma modifier appendix, or add the name to extra_modifiers if your pipeline defines it.

  • Default severity: error
  • Scope: rule
  • Fires on 0 of the corpus (0.0%)
  • Options: extra_modifiers (default [])

docs.title: Turning a check off
docs.text:
In .detection-rule-gate.yml:

checks:
  missing-falsepositives: off
  attack-technique-missing: error

For one rule, in the rule file, with a reason that is not optional:

# drg:ignore unbounded-selection reason: allowlist detection, breadth is the design

docs.title: What the checks got wrong, and how that was found
docs.text:
A linter is judged on the findings it does not raise. The firing rates in checks.md are measured automatically and reproduce on every run; whether each finding is correct cannot be measured and was assessed by hand, one rule at a time, against the pinned public corpus of 3,799 Sigma rules.

Three of the original check designs were wrong. All three were wrong in the same direction: they flagged correct Sigma, and the only way to find out was to read every finding. That is written up here rather than quietly fixed, because the failure rate of a check is the number that decides whether a team keeps the gate turned on, and a tool that does not publish it is asking to be trusted on the strength of its own description.

docs.title: 1. The wildcard check: 9 findings, 8 of them wrong
docs.text:
The first version flagged any value that was a bare asterisk. It raised 9 findings across 8 files. Reading all 9:

rule the selection verdict kubernetes_audit_hostpath_mount verb: create, objectRef.resource: pods, hostPath: '*' correct Sigma kubernetes_audit_privileged_pod_creation verb: create, objectRef.resource: pods, capabilities: '*' correct Sigma aws_ec2_vm_export_failure errorMessage\|contains: '*' inside filter1 correct Sigma aws_ec2_vm_export_failure errorCode\|contains: '*' inside filter2 correct Sigma aws_new_lambda_layer_attached two named fields plus requestParameters.layers\|contains: '*' correct Sigma aws_rds_change_master_password two named fields plus masterUserPassword\|contains: '*' correct Sigma win_security_petitpotam_susp_tgt_request EventID: 4768, TargetUserName\|endswith: $, CertThumbprint\|contains: '*' correct Sigma win_security_susp_ldap_dataexchange EventID: 5136, an attribute name list, AttributeValue\|contains: '*' correct Sigma posh_pm_alternate_powershell_hosts ContextInfo\|contains: '*' and nothing else worth raising

Eight of the nine are the same idiom. In Sigma, field: '*' is how you say this field is present and not empty. It is a constraint, not an absent one, and it is the only way to express a field existence test in rules written before the exists modifier was widely supported. Flagging it is flagging correct content.

The two AWS filter cases are worse than merely wrong. Those wildcards sit inside selections that the condition subtracts: selection and not 1 of filter*. A wildcard there excludes every event that has the field populated. The check was reporting, as too broad, two rules that the construct made narrower.

An 89% false positive rate is not a check that needs tuning. It is a check whose first lesson to a team is which flag turns the gate off.

docs.title: What the check does now
docs.text:
A finding is raised only when both of these hold:

  1. The condition makes the selection sufficient on its own. Evaluated by parsing the condition into a tree and asking whether it holds with that selection true and every other selection false, which is the state of an event that matches the selection and trips none of the rule's filters.
  2. Every constraint in that selection is unbounded. One wildcard among three named fields is an existence test; a selection whose only constraint is a wildcard matches everything the log source emits.

The first condition is what rules out the negated filters. The second is what rules out the existence idiom. Both were needed; either alone still gets the wrong answer on part of the set above.

On the same corpus the check now raises 1 finding, the last row of the table. That rule's only positive constraint is that ContextInfo is not empty, subtracting an allowlist of known PowerShell hosts. It matches every event in its log source minus that list, which is a deliberate design for that kind of detection and still a thing the author should have to state out loud. That is what suppressions with a mandatory reason are for, and tests/fixtures/clean/allowlist_with_suppression.yml is that rule's shape with the reason written down.

docs.title: 2. The modifier check: 3 findings, all wrong
docs.text:
The first version checked field modifiers against a set I wrote from memory. It raised 3 findings, all of them TargetFilename|re|i or CommandLine|re|i, and all three were valid: i, m and s are sub-modifiers of re in the Sigma specification, and my set did not have them.

An allowlist written from memory is a false positive generator with a delay built in. The set is now transcribed from the specification appendix at the commit recorded in sources.md, which also turned up that gzip, which I had assumed was a modifier, is not one.

The check now raises 0 findings on the corpus, and it knows that i is valid only directly after re, so a bare CommandLine|i is still caught.

docs.title: 3. The placeholder check: never shipped
docs.text:
A planned check looked for unreplaced %placeholder% tokens. Counting them across the corpus first:

     15 %COMSPEC%        12 %temp%        11 %AppData%      6 %dc_machine_accounts%
     13 %tmp%            12 %Public%       8 %systemroot%   6 %dc_ip_addresses%

Most are Windows environment variables being matched deliberately in a command line. Only the last two are Sigma placeholders, and those are correct as written: a placeholder is resolved by the processing pipeline at deploy time, so finding one in source is not a finding at all.

The check was dropped before it was written. The effort went into the modifier check instead, which catches a failure that is genuinely silent.

docs.title: Why the error severity checks all report zero
docs.text:
Six checks fire on nothing in this corpus: both condition checks, both duplicate checks, missing-rule-id and unknown-field-modifier. That is the correct result, not a sign they do not work. SigmaHQ runs its own validation in CI, so content that reaches the published corpus has already had every one of these caught.

They are not there for SigmaHQ's corpus. They are there for the fork a team maintains, where rules are copied as starting points, identifiers are left behind, modifiers are typed from memory and nobody runs SigmaHQ's CI. Each one is exercised by a fixture in tests/fixtures/violations/.

docs.title: How to reproduce any of this
docs.text:
make corpus          # fetch the corpus at the pinned commit
make bench           # firing rates and throughput into docs/metrics.json
drg check .corpus/sigma/rules --fail-on off --rationale

The corpus pin only moves in a commit that also updates docs/metrics.json, so the numbers and the content they were measured against cannot drift apart.

docs.title: What this does not do
docs.text: Each entry says what triggers building it, so the list is a set of decisions rather than a set of excuses.

docs.title: Multi document rule collections
docs.text:
Sigma allows several documents in one file, with action: global sharing fields across them. This tool raises rule-unparseable on such a file rather than linting the first document and reporting the file as clean, which would pass a file whose second half was never read.

The pinned corpus of 3,799 rules contains none, so the handling is covered by fixtures only.

Trigger: the first rule corpus this is pointed at that uses them.

docs.title: Correlation rules
docs.text:
Sigma correlation rules describe a relationship between other rules rather than a detection over events. They have their own specification, their own keys, and none of the checks here apply to them. They parse as rule-invalid, which is accurate but unhelpful.

The pinned corpus contains none.

Trigger: the same, plus a decision about what any of these checks would even mean for a correlation rule.

docs.title: Field name validation
docs.text:
The tool does not know whether TargetFilename exists in the log source a rule declares. A misspelled field is as silent as a misspelled modifier and a good deal more common, and catching it would be the single most valuable check here.

It needs a field taxonomy per log source, the SigmaHQ logsource guides are the obvious source, and the hard part is not the data but what to do when a team's pipeline renames fields. A check that fires on every rule in an estate with a field mapping layer is the false positive problem from false-positives.md again, at a larger scale.

Trigger: a design for reading the field mapping out of a pipeline config, rather than guessing at it.

docs.title: Changed files only
docs.text:
Every run reads every rule under the given paths. On the pinned corpus that is 1.6 seconds for 3,799 rules, so the saving would be small for most teams.

The real obstacle is that duplicate-rule-id has a corpus scope and cannot see a clash against a rule that is not in the set being checked. A changed files mode has to decide what a corpus scope check means when the corpus is a diff, and that deserves its own decision rather than being settled inside a performance change.

This already affects the pre-commit hook, which is passed only staged files and therefore cannot catch a duplicate identifier against an unstaged rule. That is why CI runs the whole tree as well.

Trigger: a corpus over about 20,000 rules, where a full run stops being cheap enough to ignore.

docs.title: Autofix
docs.text:
Several findings are mechanical: a missing identifier can be generated, and a tactic tag could be paired with its technique from a lookup table.

Not in this version. An autofix that writes to detection content is a tool that edits the thing a team is paid to be careful about, and the first version of the wildcard check in this repository would have been confidently wrong on eight rules out of nine. An autofix built on a check that has not earned trust yet is a way of propagating a mistake faster.

Trigger: a rule corpus over 200 rules where the mechanical findings are the bulk of the backlog, and at least one release where the relevant checks raised no false positives.

docs.title: Severity by rule directory
docs.text:
A team usually wants stricter rules for production content than for a scratch directory. Right now exclude is all or nothing per path.

Trigger: asked for once by anyone with a directory layout this does not serve.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text: The tool does not convert rules, and does not check that a rule converts. A rule that passes every check here can still fail in sigma convert for reasons specific to a backend. That is pySigma's job and it is good at it; running both is the right answer, and this gate is the cheaper of the two to run on every commit.

docs.title: Where the facts in this repository come from
docs.text: Every list of allowed values in this tool is a claim about the Sigma specification, and a wrong one produces false positives on correct content. The modifier allowlist was wrong the first time, written from memory, which is recorded in false-positives.md. This file is what makes the second version checkable.

docs.title: The specification
docs.text:
what source pinned at Field modifiers SigmaHQ/sigma-specification, specification/sigma-appendix-modifiers.md ba9251aa834b11a70dbf80836b453dba99c5159e Rule fields, levels, statuses SigmaHQ/sigma-specification, specification/sigma-rules-specification.md, version 2.1.0 same commit

The modifier set in src/drg/checks/modifiers.py is grouped exactly as the appendix groups it, so the two can be read side by side:

  • Generic: all, startswith, endswith, contains, exists, cased, neq
  • String: windash
  • Regular expression: re, with sub-modifiers i, m, s
  • Encoding: base64, base64offset, utf16le, utf16be, utf16, wide
  • Numeric: lt, lte, gt, gte
  • Time: minute, hour, day, week, month, year
  • Network: cidr
  • Specific: expand, fieldref

Two things worth noting from the transcription. The regular expression flags are sub-modifiers rather than modifiers, so they are valid only directly after re, and the check enforces that. And gzip, which I had assumed was a modifier, is not in the specification at all.

A pipeline that defines its own modifier is normal, and the check takes an extra_modifiers option rather than requiring a fork.

docs.title: The rule corpus
docs.text:
what source pinned at 3,799 rules SigmaHQ/sigma e3f466211866e92553d8389d621ed13cfed5523d

Not vendored. tools/fetch_corpus.py holds the pin and reproduces the exact tree; .gitignore keeps it out of the repository. Copying 3,799 third party YAML files in would bury this project's own code in the language bar, put somebody else's content in every diff, and make the corpus something that has to be updated by hand.

Rules are read from rules, rules-emerging-threats, rules-threat-hunting, rules-compliance, rules-placeholder and rules-dfir, which is every rule directory the project publishes.

docs.title: Keeping the numbers and the corpus together
docs.text:
The pin moves only in a commit that also updates docs/metrics.json. That keeps the firing rates in checks.md and the corpus they were measured against from drifting apart, which is the usual way a published benchmark becomes a historical artefact that still reads as current.

docs/metrics.json records the corpus commit alongside every number, so any figure in this repository can be traced to the tree it came from.

docs.title: No simulated numbers
docs.text:
Every figure published in this repository was produced by running this tool over the real corpus above. Nothing here is simulated, modelled or estimated, and there is no synthetic data generator in this project, so no number needs the "measured from a simulation" label that would otherwise belong next to it.

The one quantity that was measured and then deliberately withheld is the dependency install time, because repeating it gave results an order of magnitude apart. ADR-001 has the readings and the reasoning, and CI measures it on a runner instead.

docs.title: What is not sourced from anywhere
docs.text: The default severity of each check. Those were set from measured firing rates on the corpus above, and the reasoning is in checks.md. They are a judgement about what a team will tolerate on day one, not a fact about Sigma, and a team is expected to change them.

docs.title: ADR-001: Budget the dependencies, and refuse to publish the timing
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This tool installs on every pull request that touches detection content. A composite GitHub Action runs pip install on a fresh runner each time, so every dependency is a download, an import and a supply chain edge paid continuously rather than once.

The three preceding projects in this portfolio all use Typer for their command line, and copying that choice here was the path of least resistance. Before doing so I tried to measure what it costs.

docs.title: What I tried to measure, and why it is not in this document
docs.text:
The first measurement compared cold installs into fresh virtual environments:

baseline (empty venv)                5.67s   13MB
pyyaml                               0.90s   16MB
pyyaml + typer                      15.72s   31MB
pyyaml + typer + pydantic           16.39s   41MB

Typer appeared to cost roughly fifteen seconds per run. That is a large and decisive looking number, and it is noise. Repeating the same four installs three times:

rep1  pyyaml                2.15s     rep1  pyyaml typer         39.87s
rep2  pyyaml                2.61s     rep2  pyyaml typer         14.76s
rep3  pyyaml                8.24s     rep3  pyyaml typer          2.85s

The same specification took 2.85s, 14.76s and 39.87s. The spread within one specification is an order of magnitude wider than any gap between specifications, because the wall clock here is dominated by network and proxy variance rather than by the packages. The first table measured the network.

So no install timing is published anywhere in this repository. The CI workflow runs a startup job that times both install paths on a GitHub runner, where the network is the one that actually matters to a user, and writes the result to the run summary rather than into the README. A number in a README that was measured somewhere nobody runs the tool is worse than no number.

docs.title: The same lesson, later, at a smaller scale
docs.text:
The throughput benchmark has the same shape of problem in miniature. Repeating a five pass median over the corpus gave 1.594s and then 1.686s, a 6% move, and the published figure had been written to four significant figures. Not noise on the scale of the install timing, but more than enough to fail a number check for no reason and more precision than the measurement supports.

So the README publishes throughput rounded, with no verification marker, and says why. The markers are on the counts, which are deterministic: the same corpus produces the same 1,439 findings every run. A number worth checking automatically has to be a number that does not move on its own.

docs.title: What is measurable
docs.text:
Installed size and dependency count were identical across every repetition:

dependencies packages installed installed size pyyaml, pydantic 6 26MB pyyaml, pydantic, typer 13 41MB

Typer brings click, rich, pygments, markdown-it-py, mdurl, shellingham and annotated-doc: seven additional packages and 15MB, in exchange for argument parsing. This tool has three subcommands and no interactive output. argparse in the standard library does all of it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Depend on pyyaml and pydantic and nothing else. Use argparse for the command line.

Keep pydantic. It is six packages against four and the structural validation it gives is the boundary the whole design rests on, with error locations that arrive as path tuples the mark index can turn into line numbers without any translation. A hand rolled validator would be a few hundred lines reproducing that badly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The command line is more verbose to write than it would be with a decorator based parser. That cost is paid once by me, in one file, rather than on every run by every engineer whose pull request this gate inspects.

There is no coloured output and no shell completion, both of which rich and shellingham would have provided. Neither matters in a CI log, which is where this output is read.

The dependency check in tools/check_dependencies.py fails the build on any declared dependency nothing imports, so this budget is enforced rather than merely written down. That check has now found an unused declared dependency in all four repositories it has run in.

docs.title: Related: composite action rather than a Docker action
docs.text: Same reasoning, on the evidence available. A Docker action pulls or builds an image on every run; a composite action starts in the runner's own Python. I cannot measure the image pull from this environment, because the registry is unreachable from it, and so no comparison is claimed. The decision rests on what the composite action avoids rather than on a number I do not have: no image to build, publish, pin, scan or keep patched, and no registry authentication on a runner. If the startup CI job later shows the pull is cheap, the only thing that changes is that a Docker action becomes an option, not that this one became wrong.

docs.title: ADR-002: Use libyaml when it is present, and prove the two loaders agree
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The gate runs on every pull request that touches detection content, so its runtime is a cost paid continuously by every engineer on the team rather than once by whoever installed it.

A profile of a run over the pinned public corpus of 3,799 rules, taken before any attempt to make it faster, put the time almost entirely in one place:

   ncalls  tottime  cumtime  function
        1    0.191   26.678  engine.run
     3799    0.041   24.551  rules.marks.load
     3799    0.014   22.760  yaml.composer.get_single_node
  1847463    1.525   16.646  yaml.scanner.check_token
   355600    0.886   12.310  yaml.scanner.fetch_more_tokens

24.5 of 26.7 seconds was inside marks.load, and 22.8 of that was PyYAML's pure Python scanner and composer. Not one check appeared in the top eighteen entries, and neither did the condition parser, which three separate checks each call on the same string. The redundant condition parsing that looked like the obvious inefficiency was not worth finding.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Load with yaml.CSafeLoader, the libyaml binding, when it is available, and fall back to yaml.SafeLoader when it is not.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Measured over five passes on the same corpus and the same machine:

loader median spread rules/s per 1000 rules SafeLoader (pure Python) 8.557s 8.211s to 8.632s 444 2.252s CSafeLoader (libyaml) 1.594s 1.497s to 1.831s 2,383 0.420s

5.4 times faster, with findings byte for byte identical: 1,439 before, 1,439 after. Peak memory was unchanged at roughly 85 MiB, so this bought time without spending space.

The fallback is not decoration. libyaml is absent on plenty of machines, and a gate that only works where it is installed is worse than a gate that is slower, because the failure arrives as a confusing install error rather than as a longer run. The fallback is exercised by the test suite rather than assumed.

docs.title: The risk this change actually carried
docs.text:
The speed was never the question. The question was whether the two loaders report the same positions, because every finding this tool emits is anchored to a line and a loader that numbered lines differently would move every annotation in a pull request to the wrong place. That is a correctness bug wearing a performance change as a disguise, and it would not show up in any test of whether the findings were right.

So the two are compared rather than trusted:

  • Across all 3,799 rules of the pinned corpus, both loaders produce identical mark indexes, identical constructed data and identical duplicate key records. 0 mismatches of 3,799 files compared.
  • On every fixture in this repository, the same comparison runs in the test suite on every commit, including the fixtures that fail to parse, where the reported line number is compared too.
  • The five classes of parse failure (an unprintable byte, bad indentation, a multi document stream, an empty document, an unresolvable tag) produce the same exception class, the same markedness and the same reported line under both loaders.

One of those tests asserts that libyaml is present in the environment the suite runs in. Without it the comparisons compare a loader with itself and prove nothing, and a vacuous test that passes is worse than no test.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Cache the parsed condition. The suspicion before profiling was that three checks re-parsing the same condition string was the cost. The profile shows the condition parser is not in the top eighteen entries, so this would have been work spent on something that was never slow. Left alone, and the independence of the checks is worth more than the saving would have been.

Require libyaml. Would remove the fallback and its tests. Rejected: it moves a performance concern into an installation failure, and on a composite action that installs on every run it would make the gate fail on runners where the wheel is unavailable.

Parse only the files a pull request changed. A real and much larger saving, and the right thing eventually.
